Mars did have a global magnetic field for at least the first billion years of it's history. It's not a problem of lacking the right material in the core. It's something else.

It has not completely cooled. In fact, it's barely cooled at all, just like the Earth's. Mars' core, like the Earth's, contains enough radioactive material to say warm for billions of years. The reason for the loss of the martian magnetic field is somewhat of a mystery but it is not because the core is not molten. Mars' core is hot and molten just like that of the Earth. It's more likely because a major impact early in Mars' history disrupted a critical heat gradient necessary to keep core material moving in a way that produces magnetism.

Further, people often assume that Mars no longer has a molten core because of a lack of volcanic activity. This is also not the case. Because Mars doesn't have plate tectonics (or, very little plate tectonics, technically), Mars experiences long periods of no volcanic activity, interspersed by periods of major volcanic activity where core heat is released via flood basalts or through hotspots under massive shield volcanoes (like Olympus Mons). We are observing one of those long periods of no volcanic activity.
